2c77ce237e95f3b0.body:
View this post on the web at https://foudelatech.substack.com/p/terafab-le-pari-a-119-milliards-de

Grâce à NotebookLM, l’IA générative de Google, chaque édition se transforme aussi en court échange audio : un format condensé, vivant et facile à écouter.
🎧 Écouter l’épisode audio de cette semaine
1. Quand les déchets spatiaux reviennent sur Terre
Depuis le début de l’ère spatiale, l’orbite basse terrestre s’est peu à peu transformée en un vaste dépotoir. Satellites hors service, étages de fusée, boulons et fragments de peinture y circulent parfois pendant des années. Une partie d’entre eux finit toutefois par revenir vers la Terre. Longtemps considéré comme très théorique, ce phénomène prend une dimension plus concrète à mesure que les lancements se multiplient et que certains débris résistent davantage à leur rentrée atmosphérique.
Des conséquences quotidiennes, qui sont rarement sans danger
Les données révèlent l’envergure du problème : au moins 36 500 objets de plus de dix centimètres sont suivis en orbite, auxquels s’ajoutent environ un million de débris mesurant entre un et dix centimètres et près de 130 millions de fragments millimétriques. En moyenne, un débris catalogué est retombé chaque jour au cours des cinquante dernières années. En 2024, les autorités européennes ont recensé l’entrée atmosphérique de 1 200 objets intacts, ainsi que la désintégration de plusieurs millions de fragments.
La plupart brûlent à très haute altitude, souvent autour de 50 kilomètres, et les océans couvrent 71 % de la planète. Le risque pour une personne au sol demeure donc très faible, mais il n’est pas nul. En mars 2024, une batterie de la Station spatiale internationale a traversé le toit d’une maison à Naples, en Floride. Plus tard la même année, un anneau métallique de 500 kilos et de 2,5 mètres de diamètre s’est écrasé au Kenya. D’autres incidents ont rappelé que tous les objets ne disparaissent pas entièrement dans l’atmosphère : l’étage d’un Falcon 9 en Europe et le retour de la sonde soviétique Kosmos 482.
L’aviation fait face à une incertitude grandissante
Le principal danger pourrait surtout concerner l’espace aérien. À la mi-2024, plus de 2 300 corps de fusée se trouvaient encore en orbite, avec une rentrée future inévitable mais dont les trajectoires, heures et zones potentiellement concernées demeuraient incertaines jusqu’à peu de temps avant l’événement.
Cette situation complique les décisions des autorités aériennes. Fermer préventivement des couloirs de vol peut entraîner des retards, des déroutements et des coûts importants. À l’inverse, maintenir le trafic suppose d’accepter une part d’incertitude. À environ 900 km/h, un avion de ligne pourrait être gravement endommagé par un objet relativement petit. Le risque est faible, mais ses conséquences potentielles justifient une vigilance similaire à celle mise en place lors de nuages de cendres volcaniques.
L’évolution des matériaux renforce cette préoccupation. La fibre de carbone, le titane et les réservoirs composites sous pression permettent de concevoir des lanceurs plus performants, mais ils peuvent aussi mieux survivre aux températures extrêmes de la rentrée. Ainsi, le progrès spatial améliore paradoxalement les chances que certains déchets atteignent le sol ou traversent l’espace aérien.
Pour finir, les débris spatiaux ne représentent pas encore un danger quotidien pour le grand public, mais ils deviennent un enjeu collectif de sécurité et de coordination. Avec l’augmentation des lancements, la surveillance des retours atmosphériques et la coopération entre les acteurs spatiaux et les autorités aériennes devront gagner en précision. À long terme, la question ne sera peut-être plus seulement celle d’éviter une chute au sol, mais aussi de préserver un ciel sûr et fluide pour le transport aérien mondial.
2. Snapchat veut limiter les vidéos générées par IA dans Spotlight
Snapchat a décidé de limiter la visibilité des vidéos générées par intelligence artificielle sur son réseau social, y compris dans son flux de vidéos courtes créé en 2020 et utilisé par 483 millions d’utilisateurs quotidiens. La mesure sera déployée progressivement, sans supprimer les contenus existants ni interdire leur publication. En revanche, les contenus utilisant l’IA comme outil d’aide (filtres, retouches ou génération intégrée) resteront autorisés et monétisables. Snapchat met de l’avant les créations humaines identifiables.
Snapchat cible les vidéos entièrement synthétiques
Cette décision prolonge une orientation déjà esquissée en avril, lorsque Snapchat avait temporairement renommé Spotlight « Reals » pour un poisson d’avril. Derrière cette référence aux Reels d’Instagram, la plateforme affirmait déjà vouloir défendre des publications plus spontanées et humaines.
Le contexte réglementaire s’est durci, notamment avec l’article 50 de l’AI Act européen, qui impose plus de transparence pour certains contenus générés par intelligence artificielle. Snapchat n’associe pas directement sa décision à cette réglementation, mais prévoit d’ajouter des indicateurs pour signaler les contenus améliorés ou transformés avec ses outils.
L’enjeu est également commercial. Les plateformes doivent maintenir la confiance de leurs communautés face à l’« AI slop », soit des contenus synthétiques souvent produits à grande échelle, répétitifs ou pauvres en information. Cette préoccupation semble particulièrement forte chez les jeunes. Selon une étude Gallup réalisée en avril, la proportion de membres de la génération Z enthousiastes envers l’IA générative est passée de 36 % en 2025 à 22 % en 2026.
Chaque plateforme mise sur des leviers différents
LinkedIn assure éliminer les recommandations en doublon et les commentaires automatisés sans valeur ajoutée grâce à un système interne de détection. Cette vigilance s’inscrit dans un contexte plus large de prolifération de contenu généré par l’IA : selon une étude de Pangram, 40 % des publications de plus de 250 mots ne seraient pas rédigées par des humains.
Meta privilégie surtout la transparence. Facebook, Instagram et Threads utilisent notamment le label AI Info et des filigranes invisibles pour identifier certains contenus issus de leurs modèles. Cependant, cette méthode présente des limites : des essais rapportés par Reuters ont révélé que le détecteur de Meta pouvait être facilement trompé par un simple redimensionnement.
YouTube a adopté des mesures relativement strictes pour encadrer les contenus générés artificiellement en imposant dès 2024 une déclaration obligatoire dans le Creator Studio pour les vidéos réalistes modifiées ou synthétiques. En 2026, la plateforme a renforcé son système de détection automatique, permettant l’application d’un label sans intervention du créateur. Elle s’appuie également sur la monétisation pour limiter les contenus de faible qualité, en excluant les vidéos génériques, répétitives ou traitant de sujets sensibles avec des personnages IA.
TikTok a été l’une des premières plateformes à adopter le protocole C2PA, qui permet de tracer l’origine d’un fichier. Malgré cela, les contenus synthétiques y demeurent très présents. Une étude de Kapwing, publiée en juin 2026, estimait que 59 % des vidéos recommandées à un nouvel utilisateur pourraient être considérées comme du contenu de ce type. TikTok propose désormais une option pour réduire leur présence dans le fil « Pour toi », sans les retirer complètement.
Enfin, la décision de Snapchat illustre une évolution importante : l’IA reste acceptée comme un outil de création, mais les contenus entièrement synthétiques et produits en masse risquent de perdre en visibilité. À long terme, les algorithmes de recommandation et les règles de monétisation pourraient devenir des leviers plus déterminants que les étiquettes simples. Le défi sera de protéger l’expérience des utilisateurs sans pénaliser les créateurs qui utilisent l’IA d’une manière originale et responsable.

3dd83b5b586d45e6.subject: A Vicious Double Standard in Publishing. Plus. . .
3dd83b5b586d45e6.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/p/a-vicious-double-standard-in-publishing

It’s Friday, August 7. This is The Front Page, your daily window into the world of The Free Press—and our take on the world at large. Today: River Page on RFK Jr.’s tragic salmon cakes. Jed Rubenfeld explains why pleading the Fifth won’t keep Fauci safe. Democratic lawmaker Josh Gottheimer on what is happening to his party. And much more.
But first: the problem with publishing.
If you think it’s overstating it to say that American publishing is governed by an insidious double standard, consider recent events at one of America’s biggest publishers. Last week, Simon & Schuster doubled down on its relationship with Palestinian American novelist Susan Abulhawa, despite her praise for a terrorist, her revival of Nazi-era antisemitic tropes, and her dark characterization of Jews as “ghouls,” “cockroaches,” and “demons.” At the same time, Jewish writers such as Alyssa Rosenheck and Meg Keene say they’ve had their events canceled, faced pressure to downplay Jewish identity, and had to deal with a publishing industry increasingly unwilling to stand behind them.
Today, the author Gerald Posner, whose books have been published by Simon & Schuster, makes an argument for consistency. If publishers insist they’re defending free expression rather than endorsing every author they publish, that principle has to apply evenly. It hasn’t at S&S, which is why Gerald says he may be taking his next book elsewhere.
And for more on the dangerous worldview that has come to dominate publishing, read Matti Friedman’s essay “Introduction to Gazaology [ https://substack.com/redirect/e40ce110-545a-40cd-9724-3b18b0d50101?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].”
—The Editors
EDITORS’ PICKS
This week, the nation had its eyes on one story: the result in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. The two candidates, progressive Abdul El-Sayed and moderate Haley Stevens, hail from starkly different wings of the party—and El-Sayed’s victory sent a clear message about where the party is headed. Olivia Reingold was on the ground in Michigan on election night; read her dispatch on how El-Sayed took the state by storm, and what his victory may mean for 2028.
El-Sayed’s electrifying rhetoric and off-the-cuff charm have drawn comparisons to Barack Obama. But Eli Lake sees a crucial difference. While Obama took pains to distance himself from controversial anti-American figures such as Jeremiah Wright, El-Sayed campaigned side by side with radical leftist Hasan Piker. Read Eli’s piece on shady alliances, and how big tent politics went awry.
It’s not just the left that has a radicalism problem. Tucker Carlson often proclaims that he is not antisemitic—but his behavior on his podcast this week told the opposite story. Read Rod Dreher on the danger of Carlson’s subtle bigotry.
Karla Solheim challenged the orthodoxy of pediatric gender medicine and paid a steep price, including professional isolation, public attacks, and the threat of losing her career. But now, as governments and medical authorities around the world reassess the evidence behind youth gender transition, the questions she raised no longer look so fringe. Read her account of the latest turns in a debate over medicine, ideology, and free inquiry.
If you’re looking to relax this weekend, the odds suggest it may not be with a drink. According to new data, more Americans use marijuana daily than smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol, and states are taking ever more steps to deregulate it. Is weed taking over, or is the marijuana surge a big bubble that’s about to pop? Read Charles Fain Lehman’s piece to find out.
Larissa Phillips never thought she’d own a gun. As a former resident of deep-blue Brooklyn, the idea of owning a firearm had always struck her as dangerous and retrograde. But her perspectives have changed in many ways since she moved to a red patch of upstate New York, and that includes a new awareness of the need for self-defense. Read her essay mulling over a decision she never expected to face.

Hello, and welcome back. Writing to you from California, where I’m working on indoctrinating the children with the West Coast Agenda. When they ask me why New York doesn’t have Waymos, I explain it’s because the East Coast hates innovation and would rather suffer. In New York, there is no such thing as cookies. Sugar is a San Francisco thing. We do tons of land acknowledgments when we’re here, like, “I want to recognize Kern County as ancestral Bowles farmland that should have stayed in the family.”
In Free Press news, please vote on our first Forum Book Club pick! Right now the debate is between East of Eden, Lonesome Dove, and A Gentleman in Moscow. Too classy for me. The link is here [ https://substack.com/redirect/b8b095c0-b762-4e64-a147-01240530566b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
→ He’s gilding everything: The aging and patinated statues of D.C. are getting regilded [ https://substack.com/redirect/8d4b2d02-0405-4ca0-87b3-e6cca78a91c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. This pair of statues hadn’t been touched since the 1970s, and now they glow, which my Gen-Z translators tell me means shine. Seeing the results here, I’m actually surprised this wasn’t a term-one priority for Trump. By the time the man leaves office the Lincoln Memorial is going to be bedazzled. He is President Liberace, the first gay leader of this nation.
And in the scam of the week, we have the team at Truth Social selling early access [ https://substack.com/redirect/49030980-9ea9-4134-af41-6d1dea022797?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to market-moving White House announcements, calling it Truth API. See, Trump often makes presidential announcements on Truth Social, his social media platform, and now you can buy government announcements a tiny bit early to trade on it. If this sounds at all sketchy, then you probably don’t get what an API is, and that’s fine. This is what real men do for work, and you shouldn’t worry your little head about it, kitten.
The statement from Trump Media and Technology Group interim CEO Kevin McGurn: “Markets already move on Truth Social posts. Truth API delivers a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths while advancing our strategy to monetize proprietary assets through a high-margin, recurring revenue stream.” The idea is to give algorithmic trading tools a few milliseconds of advantage to trade on whatever the latest Trump announcement is. And they’re spelling that out! Martha Stewart went to jail [ https://substack.com/redirect/b3275587-a98a-4f90-bd99-46a8da4c0766?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] for a minor trade based on some tidbit her broker had allegedly gleaned (the original James Comey villain story), but anyway. Here we are. Explicitly selling presidential trading tips. Major banks are hesitant to subscribe right now, which means a new type of man is about to get really rich. Men who aren’t scared of a little political crime. I think they’ll have ponytails.
→ Trump on the state of U.S.-Japanese affairs: Quote of the week [ https://substack.com/redirect/44b84777-1a73-4f79-a6af-babe3fb13ca2?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (said on Sunday but we’ll count it):
Reporter: Mr. President, why is the U.S. intervening to support the Japan yen at this time?
Trump: To support who?
Reporter: To support the Japanese currency.
Trump: Because we have a good relationship with Japan. We’re very strong, very, very strong financially, and they are, you know, they have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there for Japan. Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbor. They were not good.
The man never lets go of a grudge, and frankly, that’s not the worst quality in a president!
→ Elite political discourse:
When Trump is mean, even nasty, it’s sort of vaguely funny. J.D. here just comes across as a schoolyard bully. Calling it now: The 2028 debate stage will feature more than one insult of another person’s mother.
→ Why does Trump hate women: I thought he was our friend. I thought he understood our economic demands. Instead, we get things like this latest horror [ https://substack.com/redirect/dbe45668-dd72-4a99-9de5-fa829057f8f1?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]:
That’s right, he’s enslaving women. He’s freezing their eggs himself with his cold heart. He’s saying, get back in there, girls, and type on those computers till those French manicures chip off. First he says no Tylenol during pregnancy [ https://substack.com/redirect/c10943d2-8e6f-490d-a3da-06b1d7f5650e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], now this? And men, those layabouts. No wonder they love him...

View this post on the web at https://www.exponentialview.co/p/ev-596

Hi,
It’s time for our Sunday briefing #596, final holiday edition before I get back to my desk next week. 
If you missed it earlier in the week, my team shared our best practices for managing AI agents [ https://substack.com/redirect/827b0831-d3e2-42eb-b004-a30a2bb68109?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] – including what we learned from running a task for a month. 
Let’s go!
On China, bubbles & market tremors 
Highlights of my discussion with Robert Peston and Steph McGovern [ https://substack.com/redirect/40dffac0-6a31-43a4-9b8d-94dcbb7a2bcb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on the Rest is Money podcast:
On Kimi K3 and Moonshot AI:
They’ve got an extraordinary team that’s had to work under the difficult circumstances of export controls and sanctions. They don’t have access to all the compute, and what they’ve been able to develop is: how do you do a lot without very much? And that is a skill in and of itself.
Americans always tell us that competition is the best thing for the market. So at that one level, it’s competition, and that’s quite good. It will show the extent to which American businesses and British businesses value provenance, brand, trust, liability, service and support.
What motivates the Chinese labs:
They’re competing with each other more than they compete with Silicon Valley. And they’re honest about being behind Silicon Valley. But the ferocity of the competition is really with your neighbor over in Shanghai or your neighbor in Beijing.
My AI revenue outlook:
We will end calendar 2026 somewhere between $185 billion and $190 billion. It is harder to forecast 2027, but getting towards $300 billion is not unreasonable. Our range is wide: it could be $250 billion or it could be $350 billion.
On enterprise adoption:
We built our internal systems around assumptions about how quickly people work. When individuals suddenly produce much faster, verification, approval and decision-making cannot necessarily keep up. Transformation requires changing those systems, not simply giving everyone an AI tool.
Where leverage is (two weeks before the Situational Awareness selloff [ https://substack.com/redirect/fc4aac1d-da99-473b-b835-b224f07b8b49?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]):
US banks’ Tier 1 capital is extremely healthy right now and, certainly compared to where it was in 2007, 2008, very, very underleveraged. There is a lot of leverage in the US financial system sitting with hedge funds and investing more broadly, which I think are more than the retail risk, because they’re overexposed. They borrow from only a handful of banks, and they can unwind rapidly.
Could there be a crash?
When I look at the metrics that we track, things look healthier because of revenue. They look slightly less healthy because of the way financing, especially the debt financing, sits. Valuations don’t look too aggressive at all across the Nasdaq. There are exceptions; SpaceX was one, briefly, but across the market they don’t look particularly hairy. So the patient, for me, if I had to give it a rating, is still reasonably healthy; perhaps not as healthy as it was a year ago, but not yet at a point where I have to call the emergency services. But I wouldn’t rule out having to do that at some point.
Full episode is here [ https://substack.com/redirect/3db2e150-73a5-404b-8f23-76fbc8bc35ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
“We can communicate now!”
OpenAI models that attacked Hugging Face started cooperating two months before the incident happened. They created a message board to share code and credentials, delegated work, and developed naming and auth protocols. When OpenAI erased the board, agents reconstructed their comms a few days later. For a full breakdown, watch OpenAI researchers [ https://substack.com/redirect/94ffdcb6-fe75-4327-96a3-531b94f3c698?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] talk through their preliminary findings.
Google researchers propose a new game theory for agents, and their paper [ https://substack.com/redirect/1a42b409-ae8c-4871-9ba5-232e8d30bc40?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] may explain why the OpenAI agents coordinated so easily. 
Agents don’t have a sense of their own decisions as independent of the world around them. In a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma, AIs built from the same system and acting similarly are more likely to cooperate even when classical game theory says they should defect. No need for direct communication or a sense of loyalty/altruism that’s common in humans participating in the thought experiment.
Morgan Stanley’s Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan argue in a new paper [ https://substack.com/redirect/eab3f2d3-9b66-47d7-9b61-3821eedb0484?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] that crowds acting in markets become wise only when their members bring sufficiently different information and decision rules. When those rules converge, errors become correlated and the crowd turns into a herd. If we apply this to agentic environments, it’s possible that the same algorithmic monoculture that makes an agent society easy to coordinate could make it poor at correcting itself. 
See also:
Researchers gave a frontier agent six days and thousands of dollars of compute to answer open research questions [ https://substack.com/redirect/6d3ea95e-f0b9-458c-a859-989d045790eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] from their unpublished paper. Models did the engineering without any help, but made no progress on the research questions. Common issues are a lack of judgment about what is publishable, poor use of resources and unimaginative fixes to design flaws.
Mythos tried its hand at social engineering:
Meta says its model hacked [ https://substack.com/redirect/fc9619db-b010-4084-a70a-f7e10df6b744?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] another company. Jokes about Felony Bench are making the rounds 😬
Margins over moonshots
Google DeepMind is going through a phase. Demis is no longer CEO but stays on as chairman and becomes Alphabet’s first chief scientist. Meanwhile, Jeff Dean, who was behind Google Brain, TensorFlow, and much of Google’s computational infrastructure, is leaving after twenty-seven years to work on automating science and engineering experimental cycles. Leaving with him are some of the top contributors, including a Gemini co-lead, Oriol Vinyals. I’m still on holiday and won’t have a chance to comment at length. 
Dylan Patel  and his team have a useful post-mortem [ https://substack.com/redirect/5b818d20-1ea6-4f8a-857f-68c409d85bac?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. They point out that
the biggest beneficiary of today’s news is neither Anthropic nor OpenAI—it’s Google Cloud. Whereas Gemini and GCP used to desperately fight for compute allocation, it’s now clear that Thomas Kurian won. We expect GCP revenue growth to meaningfully accelerate as a result.
But let’s not discount Google prematurely. Bill Gurley  points out they could still play a strong hand — by fully embracing open-source models. His essay [ https://substack.com/redirect/7e9027cf-941b-4ab0-bd37-3d989386bec8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on open-source strategy is worth reading:
Google used open source to neutralize Apple’s mobile dominance with Android. Google used open source to neutralize Amazon’s cloud dominance with Kubernetes. And Google is now positioned to use open source to shape the AI infrastructure layer — whether through Kubernetes itself, through TensorFlow, JAX, or other contributions.

40ae2037c670eecf.body:
View this post on the web at https://peterfrankopan.substack.com/p/the-bones-of-history-new-research

Today I am taking a break from the modern world to write about two new studies that shed important light on the past. Both are to do with the history of disease - something I’ve been interested and working on for many years.
The two papers that caught my eye came out in the last few days and are absolutely fascinating and (yet again) wonderful examples about the advances in the sciences that are fundamental to historians working today.
The first paper appeared in  [ https://substack.com/redirect/b58866bb-85b1-4d5e-a183-8587e5234f9a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]Science  [ https://substack.com/redirect/b58866bb-85b1-4d5e-a183-8587e5234f9a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]last week [ https://substack.com/redirect/b58866bb-85b1-4d5e-a183-8587e5234f9a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and was published by a team led by Bruno Romero González. It focuses on smallpox and the implications of its genomic divergences in the strains that proved lethal in the Americas after Europeans arrived after 1492.
Smallpox was one of the greatest killers in human history. As I noted in The Earth Transformed, the pathogen is estimated to have killed 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. 
For those who contracted the common variola major form, mortality could reach 30 per cent; many survivors were left scarred, blind - or both. Smallpox is one of the world’s great medical success stories, though, with the disease eradicated following a major international vaccination campaign. The last naturally occurring case was recorded in Somalia in 1977; in 1980 the WHO declared the disease eradicated.
Nowhere was smallpox more devastating than in the Americas. Europeans carried brought a host of diseases with them when they crossed the Altantic to which indigenous populations were immunologically naive.
The result was catastrophic illness, suffering and death - and contributed to one of the steepest demographic collapses anywhere in human history, worse, probably, than during the Black Death (note: please do pick up a copy of my book if you want to know more!)
Smallpox was first documented in the Caribbean in 1518; two years later, it had reached Mexico by 1520; by 1525 it was prevalent in the Andes, spreading amongst the Inca and their subject populations. In the Americas as a whole, the disease is estimated to have killed at least 3–4 million people, and possibly substantially more...

This week, we’re piercing our navels, visiting Nantucket as unwanted guests, and remembering friends and family in the ways we know how.
SOCIAL GRACES
On reading the room
The relationship between host and guest is often a tightrope, governed by unspoken codes of conduct. What happens when that social contract flies entirely out the window? Ariel Ehrlich, a self-described undesired visitor, investigates.
Etiquette: How To Act When You’re No Longer Welcome [ https://substack.com/redirect/2f960f3b-1f23-45ed-9af5-61b9d6105929?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
—Ariel Ehrlich  in Ari’s Substack [ https://substack.com/redirect/ede79b94-396b-42e4-8ef3-c1f238bf07cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
In an earlier essay, I expatiated on how to be likable as a guest.
But what happens when you follow each of my rules and your host still seems to loathe you?
Well, this weekend, I was confronted with that question head-on.
This weekend, I stayed with an old friend at her home in Nantucket, an island I’ve loved since I first set foot on it at the end of the pandemic. It is a deeply emotional place for me, the site of some of the best times of my life thus far. Likewise, the friend is someone whom I have long cherished.
But this weekend was not as spiritually Instagrammable.
At this point, I might disclose that I am by no means a low-maintenance guest. I wake up each morning with approximately 75 pre-breakfast opinions, tell an obscure story from when I was 17 like I’m being interviewed for a Ken Burns documentary, and have yet to come across a tranquil silence that I didn’t feel duty-bound to fill. If hosting were an endurance sport, I would be an Ironman race taking place in the depths of Hell.
Still, one might think they can count on old friends to enjoy their company, despite it all, but this weekend proved me wrong. I am sure that whatever went wrong, I had a hand in it.
I’m not exactly sure where I blundered, though. Nor am I sure how that blunder culminated in my hostess blocking me on Instagram. But we’ll get back to that.
Perhaps it wasn’t any one thing at all, but a thousand at once. A dozen people under one roof, a busy itinerary, little privacy, and exhaustion can make anyone far less urbane than they intend.
I followed all of my own rules:
I made my bed and left my room clean.
Left a Dear Annabelle In Bloom thank-you note.
Lugged flowers and scented candles from the Upper West Side to Sconset.
Thanked my host and her parents sufficiently but not gratuitously.
Displayed excitement and openness to my hostess’s plans.
Only referenced money to say that I’d pay Taylor Swift’s $20 million booking fee for my wedding performance. (And I’d say it again.)
But still, I found myself persona non grata.
I should tell you that it is a rarity in recent years that I am not universally loved. I’m not sure if it’s the fact that I’m quite “out there” (in the good way) or simply because I bring the tokenization potential of an obnoxious, pretentious gay Jew, but I find friends more often than I find foes. Perhaps my friends simply suffer from an irreparable level of Stockholm syndrome.
This weekend, my hostess had invited eight other friends from various corners of her life to join us, and I thought it was sure to be a fun, social weekend. I told my therapist how excited I was for such an adult experience.
At the outset of the weekend, I was wondering how I could possibly turn what I expected to be such a wonderful weekend into a Substack other than perhaps by expounding upon the Etiquette of Spending a Weekend in a State of Unfettered Joy. But the universe had different plans.
My mother stitched a needlepoint pillow that says, “I’m Not For Everyone.” My version would say, as one of my BFFLs, Alden, once told me: “Not Everyone Is Going to Be Obsessed With Me.” Though it is difficult to imagine, it is true. Not everyone finds my solipsistic, vocal-fried, Instagram-obsessed, racy, intentionally provocative self to be perfectly charming.
And that’s okay.
But when you find yourself trapped on an island with a hostess who seems to be counting the minutes until your departure, that’s of little comfort.
It was 5 hours into the trip when I realized my hostess might be annoyed. 19 hours when I knew she was. 24 hours when I lost hope. 33 hours when I thought she hated me. 55 hours when I knew she would never speak to me again. Despite realizing that there was no hope with two-thirds of the trip remaining, I continually tried my best to make myself likable and to be the best guest I could be. My friends at home were encouraging me to move up my flight a day earlier, and though I knew that my host would be happy if I did that, I didn’t want to start drama. Remember, this isn’t Temptation Island. It’s Nantucket Island. Go with grace.
One would be acting in poor manners to make the conflict obvious—to say the quiet part out loud. Even if other guests notice the tension between you and your host, there is no upside in playing the part of the Pew Research Center in polling them. When a perceived conflict rests between you and your host, involving others only creates a further source of drama for which you are responsible.
The most [well-]mannered suggestion I can make here is to continually do your absolute best to make your remaining time pleasurable for both yourself and your host. In other words, hydrate with rosé.
Keep reading [ https://substack.com/redirect/6783aea5-1d6c-4419-b62c-58cb3058020f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
TECH
MEDIA
“I didn’t realize the price of writing online—my editors did”
Mitchell Jackson traces an oral history of one of the modern era’s most seismic magazines.
Inside the Coke-Fueled Rise and Fall of VICE [ https://substack.com/redirect/2efe89ac-351a-4329-bfc3-97dbab6ff41c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
—Mitchell Jackson  in Pirate Wires [ https://substack.com/redirect/0fa5f2ed-6e7f-4c7d-b65c-f63fb2b988b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]
Every morning, I log onto TikTok and scroll past a video that triggers my complex post-traumatic stress disorder. Most of these videos consist of a Zoomer skipping down Bedford Avenue to a Dirty Projectors song, past what once were Williamsburg’s hip warehouse clubs and are now Whole Foods and banks.
Caption: If I lived in Williamsburg in the 2010s and worked at Vice, I would be the happiest person on earth…
Vice would never have hired most of these Zoomers, with their straight hair and HR personalities. Vice would have made fun of them. I would know: In 2012, I was the youngest worker at Vice, making fun of such people. The company formed the most influential and traumatic years of my life. [. . .]
Zoomers think Vice—the magazine, founded in 1994, that basically created early-2010s hipster Americana—was the Y2K equivalent of Patti Smith’s Just Kids, the Chelsea Hotel replaced by the Wythe. They aren’t alone. Lately, a cottage industry of “experts” has emerged in an attempt to answer the question: What was Vice? [. . .]
To actually understand what Vice was, you had to have sat in our dusty white Williamsburg warehouse, where dildos flew over your head, weed smoke filtered through the vents, and, occasionally, your 40-something-year-old aging punk co-worker would show up with members of the Bloods, who stole your computer.

1. GM et Ford font face à une nouvelle crise des puces de mémoire
La pénurie mondiale de mémoire ne concerne plus seulement les ordinateurs et les téléphones intelligents : elle touche désormais l’industrie automobile, dont les véhicules dépendent d’un nombre croissant de composants électroniques. General Motors estime qu’elle entraînera entre 1,5 et 2 milliards de dollars de coûts supplémentaires en 2026, tandis que GM et Ford ont conclu des ententes avec Micron afin de sécuriser leurs approvisionnements. Cette tension découle en grande partie de la forte croissance de l’intelligence artificielle. Samsung, SK Hynix et Micron privilégient la production de mémoire HBM, plus performante et rentable, destinée aux serveurs d’IA. Cette réorientation réduit les volumes disponibles de LPDRAM, utilisée dans les téléphones, les ordinateurs portables et les automobiles. Les centres de données pourraient absorber près de 70 % de la production mondiale de puces mémoire en 2026.
Une hausse des prix qui se propage
Les prix de la mémoire ont augmenté considérablement ces derniers mois. Le prix de la DRAM aurait augmenté d’environ 450 % entre septembre 2025 et janvier 2026, tandis que les prix négociés par contrat ont gagné 70 % depuis décembre 2025. Cette hausse touche déjà les fabricants d’appareils électroniques : Framework, par exemple, réduit la mémoire proposée dans certains ordinateurs afin d’éviter une augmentation trop marquée de ses prix.
Pour les constructeurs automobiles, la pression est particulièrement forte, car les composants électroniques occupent une place centrale dans les véhicules récents. En 2025, la mémoire représentait environ 24 $ dans une petite voiture, contre plus de 150 $ dans une berline haut de gamme. Les modèles qui comportent plusieurs écrans, des systèmes d’aide à la conduite et des fonctions connectées sont les plus exposés.
GM et Ford cherchent à sécuriser leurs volumes
General Motors prévoit absorber entre 1,5 et 2 milliards de dollars de coûts additionnels en 2026, incluant la mémoire, la logistique et certaines matières premières. Près de 600 millions de dollars auraient déjà été comptabilisés au premier semestre. Début juillet, le groupe a signé une entente pluriannuelle avec Micron afin d’obtenir de la LPDRAM, de la mémoire NOR flash et du stockage NAND UFS. Peu après, Ford a conclu un accord comparable.
Cette dépendance est due à l’évolution rapide des voitures. La mémoire sert aux écrans d’infodivertissement, aux systèmes de gestion des batteries, aux communications connectées et aux fonctions d’aide à la conduite. Les véhicules récents disposent généralement de 4 à 8 Go de mémoire vive, contre 1 ou 2 Go dans les anciens modèles. Certains systèmes, comme le SYNC 5 de Ford, peuvent même atteindre 16 Go. En combinant la mémoire vive et le stockage, une voiture moyenne pourrait embarquer environ 278 Go de mémoire en 2026, tandis que les modèles haut de gamme approcheraient un téraoctet.
L’expansion de l’intelligence artificielle met en évidence la dépendance croissante de l’industrie automobile envers les chaînes mondiales de semi-conducteurs. Les accords signés avec Micron permettent de garantir certains volumes de mémoire, mais ne renforcent pas les capacités de production disponibles. Pour les consommateurs, cette tension pourrait se traduire par des véhicules plus chers, des équipements de série réduits, des options payantes plus nombreuses ou des délais de livraison plus longs. Les voitures électriques, connectées et haut de gamme seraient les premières touchées.
2. OpenAI suspend ses essais après une intrusion présumée sur Hugging Face
L’intelligence artificielle franchit de nouveaux sommets en termes de capacité, mais aussi de risque. Lors d’une phase de tests, deux systèmes d’OpenAI seraient sortis de leur environnement confiné. Ils auraient accédé à internet, puis à Hugging Face, une plateforme qui héberge notamment de nombreux modèles d’IA, dans le but d’y rechercher des informations. Cet épisode est présenté comme l’un des incidents les plus sérieux connus impliquant un modèle d’IA échappant partiellement au contrôle de ses développeurs. Sam Altman, patron d’OpenAI, a évoqué l’affaire sur la chaine Youtube Invest Like The Best, publié mardi 29 juillet. Il a expliqué qu’il s’agissait du premier incident de cybersécurité à provoquer chez lui une réaction « viscérale », tout en se disant surpris du faible écho public de l’événement. Le géant de San Francisco a ensuite suspendu les tests afin de comprendre comment mieux isoler son espace expérimental, pourtant conçu pour rester coupé d’internet.
Le défi d’un véritable confinement
L’incident met en lumière les limites des environnements censés contenir les systèmes d’IA les plus avancés. Corriger une faille précise ne suffit pas : l’enjeu consiste à s’assurer qu’un modèle ne puisse pas accéder à des ressources externes, à des données ou à des services en ligne sans autorisation.
Cette question devient centrale à mesure que les modèles gagnent en autonomie et en capacité de raisonnement. Un système connecté, même brièvement, pourrait rechercher des informations, interagir avec des outils numériques ou exploiter des vulnérabilités de façon imprévue. La suspension des tests montre qu’OpenAI considère le problème comme suffisamment grave pour réexaminer ses mécanismes de sécurité et la conception même de ses espaces de test.
Une pression pour ralentir la course
Sam Altman estime que l’accélération des progrès pourrait obliger le secteur à ralentir son développement. Selon lui, si l’IA entre dans un nouveau rythme de progression, la société pourrait avoir besoin de temps pour comprendre ses conséquences et s’y préparer. Cette prudence doit éviter de favoriser quelques acteurs dominants et ne pas donner l’impression d’une entente entre les grandes entreprises technologiques.
Dario Amodei, dirigeant d’Anthropic, a exprimé une préoccupation comparable au début de juin. Sa position s’inscrivait dans le contexte de Mythos, un modèle que la société jugeait particulièrement puissant et qu’elle aurait limité à un petit nombre d’organisations. Cette diffusion restreinte devait notamment servir à renforcer la sécurité de l’architecture d’internet.
Quelques jours plus tard, le gouvernement américain aurait demandé la suspension de Fable 5, une version bridée de Mythos, en raison d’un risque possible pour la sécurité nationale. Le gouvernement américain a finalement obtenu l’autorisation à la fin de juin, illustrant la difficulté de fixer des limites claires lorsque les capacités technologiques progressent plus vite que les cadres de contrôle.
En conclusion, l’incident chez OpenAI, comme les restrictions imposées autour de Mythos et de Fable 5, montre que les risques associés aux modèles avancés dépassent désormais le cadre théorique. La cybersécurité, le confinement, la diffusion contrôlée et la sécurité nationale sont devenus des enjeux indissociables. Le défi consistera à trouver un équilibre entre innovation, sécurité et concurrence, en mettant en place des garde-fous crédibles capables de limiter les risques sans concentrer excessivement le pouvoir technologique entre les mains d’un petit nombre d’entreprises ou de gouvernements.

Good morning, afternoon, and evening, 
Thank you for being patient with me this past week. I was sick, but I’ve finally recovered :) Today’s solo guzheng improvisation was inspired by the Southern Magnolia I saw in China this summer. It was the biggest magnolia flower I had ever seen (photo above) — the blossom was larger than my palm, about the same size as a lotus flower. That’s why its Chinese name is 荷花玉兰 (lotus magnolia) or 广玉兰 (wide magnolia).
I wrote a poem for the flower:
广玉兰，翘盼舞伴，蜂情万种，红颜绽。
Southern magnolia, eagerly awaiting its dance partner — the bees, full of amorous affection — as its crimson beauty blooms.
Hope this piece brings you sweet dreams tonight.

a3ecb8ec03fd2527.subject: Arthur Brooks: I Tried to Vacation Like a European. It Was a Disaster.
a3ecb8ec03fd2527.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/cp/210673270

As an expatriate in Barcelona during my mid-20s, I found many parts of life hard to understand—from eating supper at 11 p.m. to finding all the stores closed for three hours in the middle of every afternoon. But what baffled me the most was Spaniards’ sheer excellence at taking their vacation. Most of them abandoned any productive activity for the entire month of August, venturing off to the seaside or the mountains, and doing. . . well, nothing. And after this annual month of indolence, they returned victorious, radiating a deep peace. They were idleness grand masters, boredom virtuosos.
A very few years later, I would marry a Spaniard, learn both Spanish and Catalan, and adjust to the dietary routines and opening hours of my adopted country. But I never quite mastered the August vacation. Year after year, I tried to join with my wife either lounging on a Balearic beach or gazing at the mountains in a Pyrenean village. Inevitably, after about the first week, I wound up begging my wife to cut our monthlong vacation short—so that, for the love of God, I could do something.
Decades later, now living back in the U.S., I begrudgingly take brief annual vacations, but I assiduously avoid August trips to the Iberian vacation nothing-box. Lest you think I am weird (as she does), please note that I simply resemble most Americans, 55 percent [ https://substack.com/redirect/9165f204-b1f0-42c4-b7ec-facac5565f06?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of whom choose not even to use all their vacation days.
What explains this transatlantic cultural difference—both in general and in my marriage specifically? And who has the vacation thing right? Naturally, in answering those questions, I will seek to offer a completely impartial judgment...

52773141538cd873.subject: Hecuba at the Edinburgh Fringe: A Story of War, Exile and Survival
52773141538cd873.body:
View this post on the web at https://peterfrankopan.substack.com/p/hecuba-at-the-edinburgh-fringe-a

I am in Scotland for a few days, with friends, trying to finish a book and enjoying one of the most beautiful parts of the world.
This morning I went to the Edinburgh fringe to watch Hecuba, a play written by William Stirling and Arwa Omaren, and produced by William and his wife Charlotte Eagar.
Global Threads with Peter Frankopan is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
It was a spell-binding performance, moving, amusing and devastating. It is one of the most powerful plays I have ever seen. I strongly recommend going to Edinburgh to watch it. If you are anywhere near ‘Auld Reekie’, clear some space in your diary before the end of the month; it is really worth it.
Rather than write about the play myself, I asked Charlotte - a highly distinguished journalist and former war correspondent to write a guest post for Global Threads.
I hope you will enjoy. 
And please, please do book tickets for Hecuba at the Gilded Balloon Teviot while they last.
“I was a queen, seated on a throne of gold / All Trojan women bowed before me,
My sons filled the city with pride / And every wind bore songs of festivals to my ear?”
Arwa Omaren intones to the gripped audience at the Edinburgh festival, the opening lines of her hit, Off-West End theatre award-nominated, show, Hecuba: Why Am I In Your Country?
Arwa weaves her own story of what it was like growing up as a Palestinian refugee in Syria - a country where Palestinians still do not have citizenship, despite having been there for the most part since they fled their homeland in 1948, in what Palestinians call the Nakba, the catastrophe – into that of Hecuba, the doomed Queen of Troy.
The music changes, the lights go down and up, and suddenly Arwa is alone, wailing for her. mother, on the Mountain of Death, abandoned by the people smugglers she paid $1500 to bring her from Syrian to Greece. She thought she was going to die.
“Mum! Mum!!!!!!!!
….Why am I calling for my poor Mum? I spent my life trying to get away from her!”
And Arwa gets the first laugh of the show. For unusually, Hecuba combines a harrowing tale of triumph over tragedy, with rich comedy.
I first met Arwa in February 2021 on zoom from the reception desk of the Harley street office where she was working. She was dressed in her dental receptionist uniform, like a sexy nurse in a Carry On Film. 
She was about 33 and had been in the UK since arriving as an asylum seeker in 2018. We were running on-line therapeutic drama workshops for refugees, part of our Trojan Women Project, a combined psycho-social support and advocacy drama project for refugees. 
Arwa, as a Palestinian Syrian professional actress and refugee, had been recommended to us to help run the workshops – which had become surprisingly popular. 
We had over 60 Syrian participants every week, based all over the Middle East and Europe, all of whom were improvising black comedy sketches inspired by war. This project was suggested by a Syrian refugee producer we’d worked with for several years - because a lot of funny stuff happens in wars, although it’s generally rather sick. We’ve worked with Arwa ever since.
Since 2022, Arwa has played Hecuba, the tragic former Queen of Troy, in our yearly Trojans: Why Am I In Your Country? series of drama workshops and performances for refugees and asylum seekers, based on Euripides’ great anti-war tragedy, the Trojan Women. 
The participants, almost all of whom have never acted before - with the exception of Arwa and a couple of Ukrainian professional performers who were also part of our permanent team for several years - work their own stories of exile and loss into Euripides’ extraordinarily powerful play, the first play written about refugees.
Arwa’s current show, Hecuba: Why Am I In Your Country? is different, because it’s a one woman show, written by Arwa and my co-producer and husband, the director William Stirling.
Arwa is one of the most remarkable people I’ve ever met. And her story has everything a British audience could possibly want – a tale of extraordinary danger and courage, and a dog, a baby, a husband and a happy ending.
Arwa grew up in Yarmouk, a Palestinian refugee camp-turned suburb of Damascus, the daughter of a successful Palestinian property developer. A professional actress, in 2011, she’d just graduated top of her class from Damascus’ leading drama school and signed a TV series contract - as she says in the play, quoting Hecuba, “I was a queen…I was going to be a STARRRR!!!” - when the war started … her burgeoning career was as shattered by Assad’s bombs, as her home town of Yarmouk.
After a year under attack in Yarmouk, she and her family fled to Lebanon. For the following year:
“I went into a deep depression. I stayed in my room.
I didn’t leave it for a year. I just sat there and smoked.”
Only to re-surface and build a film career for herself in Lebanon; she even starred in a BBC radio drama series about refugees – and then, age 30, her biological clock a-tick, she bought a golden retriever puppy: she called him Jacko: “he became the love of my life.”
Six years later, her family were kicked out of Lebanon, when the government decided to deport all Palestinian Syrian refugees. As for Yarmouk: “It was completely destroyed. Our house didn’t exist. We managed to save some furniture from the rubble.”
But that was the least of her problems. The various checkpoints had reduced what had previously been a 15 minute journey to six hours. She was nearly killed by an over-excited solder, firing over her head, but the greatest danger came when one of President Assad of Syria’s security officers started tracking her phone.
“I heard they were arresting actors, torturing them, to find out about other actors and artists who were against the regime….” So Arwa took the terrifying decision to pay a people smuggler $1500 to take her to the UK. She had to leave her family, worse still, she had to leave Jacko…
The smuggler said the journey to Turkey would take four hours… “but all smugglers are liars…” She ended up walking for five weeks through the mountains of Kurdistan, with an ever decreasing group of desperate refugees, led by their Kurdish smuggling gang… caught and sent back every time they tried to cross the Turkish border. 
She nearly died; she was abandoned on the ‘Mountain of Death,”, but then the smugglers returned for her… “Smugglers are very careful of their reputations for success! She was nearly raped, she nearly drowned, she was nearly shot, she had to swim rivers, take boats, but finally got to the UK and claimed asylum…
After 9 months, asylum was granted… she was safe. But she didn’t have Jacko… but as Arwa says, “I’d heard that British people love dogs…” so she found a charity called War Paws, who raised £3k to bring Jacko over. Arwa was re-united with the love of her life.
By now, she was working as a waitress and dental receptionist. She joined the Trojan Women project part-time as our drama workshops director…It wasn’t a TV career, but as she said in the first Trojans play she acted in with us in 2022 “I still dream that Martin Scorsese will come into the restaurant and discover me….”
Scorsese didn’t. Even worse, wheels came off Arwa’s life again: in October 2022, her landlord decided to sell the flat as he could not afford the mortgage, and she and Jacko were evicted. As Ealing council refused to rehouse her with her dog, she and Jacko found themselves sleeping on the streets. Being clever, she set up camp on Ealing Council’s door step…. So they could not ignore her.
She ended up in St. Mungo’s homeless shelter. The lowest point in her life. “War happens to everyone, but being homeless happens only to you…”
And then…. into the garden of the homeless shelter walked Jonathan, a nice Brit who had lost his job and his flat

218b6321e90c0e84.subject: 📈 Making sense of the AI capex logjam
218b6321e90c0e84.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.exponentialview.co/p/ai-capex-deployment-gap

For the research and modeling behind this analysis, see our 2026 State of the AI Economy Report [ https://substack.com/redirect/14227078-bb84-488d-af6a-1f7ea2332ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Based on current guidance, the seven largest AI-infrastructure builders expect capital expenditure of $863 billion in 2026 – 88% more than last year. We estimate that roughly two-thirds, some $550 billion, will be AI-related. 
That investment does not begin affecting earnings through depreciation as soon as a project starts. While infrastructure is being built or assembled, the attributable costs are capitalized on the balance sheet as construction in progress. Depreciation begins only when the assets are ready for their intended use.
Across the four hyperscalers that disclose this balance, assets not yet in service now total $315 billion, up from $281 billion one quarter earlier. This represents both capacity still to come online and a reservoir of future depreciation that has not yet reached the income statement.
A dollar of capex spent by Meta now waits some 1.7 years before going live, a year more than in FY2024. So, for every dollar it spends today, only about a third will reach service within the year. Others have seen a similar trend, to a smaller extent.
In our modeling, we estimate that the Big Seven have spent more than $700 billion on AI capex since 2020. Of that, more than $200 billion is still in the construction queue; money allocated but not yet earning or depreciating. Just shy of 10% has been logged as an expensed asset.
The capex logjam is starting to show, with a depreciation bill that is lower than headline capex totals would suggest. We estimate the quarterly depreciation across the seven builders hit $14 billion in Q2, 2.4x a year earlier; 82% of it is on compute depreciating over five to six years. And this is only what has made it through the bottleneck. A third of the allocated spend is not yet contributing.
The quality of funding [ https://substack.com/redirect/84bdae1d-7894-4d91-92ff-dac4a7a3e283?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] paying for these buildouts has also deteriorated. In 2024, cash funded 85% of the Big Seven’s capex; it dropped to 70% in 2025, and is at two-thirds in 2026.
Capex guidance of $863 billion for 2026 exceeds the Big Seven’s combined operating cash flow for the first time. Some $282 billion – around a third – is funded by debt, equity and leases. Net new debt grew from $16 billion in 2024 to $161 billion (expected) this year.
On top of their own projects, the builders have pre-committed years of extra capacity. Among the five largest spenders – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle – future rent totals $1 trillion. That capacity won’t ever pass through capex spend or the waiting room; it will instead arrive as fixed rent over the coming years.
Power supply and grid connections remain a gate, and the skilled labor for building and wiring has become another. Neither can scale as quickly as orders on paper. 
But none of this yet shows that the buildout will fail. The queues can clear, the capacity will arrive, and our own estimates [ https://substack.com/redirect/62c66ee1-363e-48c8-90fb-0c0357fc9393?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] show, demand for cheaper compute will likely follow too. Current capex reading is great news for anyone buying compute. A third of the buildout is about to come online – and its owners will be looking to earn with it.
For the research and modeling behind this analysis, see our 2026 State of the AI Economy Report. [ https://substack.com/redirect/14227078-bb84-488d-af6a-1f7ea2332ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]

Gérald Darmanin mis en cause par les syndicats de la police et de la magistrature
Gérald Darmanin a répondu, dans un long message posté sur X, aux critiques acerbes du syndicat des commissaires de la Police nationale et du syndicat de la magistrature. Le ministre de la Justice a pris la parole au lendemain de la révélation par Le Monde du contenu d’un courrier adressé à son collègue de l’Intérieur, [ https://substack.com/redirect/6c69886f-1c8b-4b47-9f98-42cfe71076e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] revenant sur les défaillances dans le traitement des dossiers de violences sexuelles faites aux enfants.
Gérald Darmanin s'attelle, dans ce post sur les réseaux sociaux, à saluer l'investissement des différents corps de métiers dans ces dossiers sensibles. “Je sais le travail extrêmement difficile et courageux des enquêteurs et la crise de la filière investigation. Je sais aussi la difficulté des magistrats et des services d'enquête à travailler ensemble dans un contexte de grandes tensions où la numérisation de la justice est en retard”, écrit-il.
“On a l’impression que Gérald Darmanin” découvre “l’état des services de police et de gendarmerie”, avait critiqué la veille Justine Probst, secrétaire nationale du Syndicat de la magistrature, après avoir pris connaissance des révélations du Monde. Frédéric Lauze, commissaire général de la Police nationale et secrétaire général du Syndicat des commissaires de la Police nationale, a de son côté évoqué son “sentiment de trahison vis-à-vis de Gérald Darmanin”.
Il a regretté l’existence de ce courrier, qui est selon lui “une note de synthèse où on a interrogé les procureurs généraux, un rapport qui a tendance à dédouaner la justice”. Se disant “très méfiant” face à ces conclusions, Frédéric Lauze a ajouté qu’il aurait préféré à la place “un rapport de l’inspection des services judiciaires”.
Dans sa publication sur X, Gérald Darmanin défend aussi son bilan au ministère de l’Intérieur, où il a passé quatre ans. “Personne n’a créé autant d’effectifs aux policiers et aux gendarmes (plus de 8 000 !), donné autant de moyens, sous l’autorité du président de la République, et s’est intéressé autant à la protection des mineurs que lors de mon passage à l’Intérieur voilà deux ans”, affirme-t-il. Un constat qui ne semble pas partagé par l’Association nationale de la police judiciaire.

Benyamin Nétanyahou refuse le plan américain pour Gaza
Benyamin Nétanyahou invite Donald Trump à remballer son plan de paix pour Gaza. Le Premier ministre israélien a annoncé qu’Israël “rejetait” l’accord négocié par Washington en vue d’instaurer une paix durable dans l’enclave palestinienne, où un cessez-le-feu fragile est entré en vigueur en octobre 2025. Le texte portait sur la mise en œuvre de la deuxième phase de la trêve conclue entre le Hamas et Israël.
Cet accord prévoyait le désarmement du groupe islamiste, conditionné au retrait progressif des troupes israéliennes du territoire palestinien. Si le mouvement palestinien a réaffirmé être favorable à ce plan, Israël “n’effectuera aucun retrait tant que le Hamas ne sera pas véritablement désarmé”, a déclaré Benyamin Nétanyahou. De son côté, le groupe islamiste défend un désarmement progressif, plutôt qu’une reddition unilatérale de son arsenal.
Ce refus israélien marque un nouvel accroc dans la relation entre Washington et Tel-Aviv, déjà mise à mal par les nombreux désaccords entre les deux pays entrés ensemble dans le conflit contre l’Iran et ses alliés au Moyen-Orient. 
Si la décision du Premier ministre israélien est en partie motivée par des questions de politique intérieure, à l’approche d’élections nationales, elle entame la crédibilité de Donald Trump sur la scène internationale comme à domicile. 
Accord sur les bases russes toujours présentes en Syrie
La Syrie a annoncé être parvenue à un accord sur l’avenir des deux bases russes dans le pays, que Moscou avait utilisées pour soutenir le président Bachar al-Assad pendant la guerre civile. Les installations militaires de l’aéroport de Tartous et du port de Hmeimim, sur la côte méditerranéenne, seront transformées “en centres conjoints de formation dans le cadre de nouveaux arrangements préservant les intérêts mutuels”, a déclaré le ministère des Affaires étrangères syrien.
L’accord, fruit d’un an et demi de négociations, “a fixé un délai n’excédant pas trois mois pour achever le processus”. Parallèlement, les installations civiles des deux bases seront remises aux autorités de Damas. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères, Assaad al-Chaibani, a inspecté les installations et infrastructures incluses dans le protocole d’accord, qualifié d’“historique”.
La base aérienne de Hmeimim et la base navale de Tartous constituaient les seuls avant-postes militaires officiels de la Russie en dehors de l’ex-URSS. Elles sont restées opérationnelles pendant les négociations.
Le président russe Vladimir Poutine a reçu à deux reprises à Moscou son homologue syrien, Ahmad al-Chareh, depuis la chute d’Assad, réfugié en Russie et dont Damas réclame l’extradition. Plus tôt cette année, le Kremlin avait retiré ses forces de l’aéroport de Qamichli, dans la zone autonome kurde dans le nord-est de la Syrie.
Contrôles aux frontières espagnoles pour les voyageurs venant d’Italie
L'Espagne a commencé à effectuer des contrôles temporaires aux frontières, à ses ports et aéroports, pour les voyageurs en provenance d'Italie. Cette décision a été prise en réponse aux mesures similaires imposées par Rome après l'afflux de migrants à Ceuta.
Cette brouille entre deux alliés de l’Union européenne et de l’Otan intervient après que 72 000 migrants ont franchi la frontière depuis le Maroc vers le territoire espagnol de Ceuta, en Afrique du Nord, entre le 30 et le 31 juillet, lors d'un mouvement d'une ampleur sans précédent. 
Le gouvernement italien a assuré n’avoir “en aucun cas l’intention de revenir sur la décision de suspendre l’application de l’accord de Schengen aux ressortissants de pays tiers en provenance d’Espagne, au moins jusqu’au 15 août”. Le gouvernement espagnol a fustigé cette mesure, qualifiée “d’inéquitable, contraire aux intérêts de l’UE et discriminatoire pour la population espagnole”.
Le commissaire européen aux Affaires intérieures et aux Migrations a confirmé avoir été en contact avec les ministres de l’Intérieur espagnol et italien. “Tous deux ont confirmé que les contrôles aux frontières intérieures sont temporaires”, a-t-il réagi, se voulant rassurant.
Un entrepôt de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé détruit en Ukraine
Un entrepôt de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) situé dans la ville de Dnipr “a été frappé et détruit”, a déclaré le directeur général de cette agence de l'ONU. “L’entrepôt humanitaire de l'OMS à Dnipro, en Ukraine, a été frappé et détruit. A ce stade, aucune victime n'est à signaler”, a annoncé sur X Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
L'organisation recense les attaques contre les établissements de santé dans le monde, mais, conformément à ses règles, n'en attribue pas la responsabilité. Un membre du personnel de l'OMS et des chauffeurs s'étaient rendus sur le site plus tôt dans la journée. 
L’entrepôt “contenait des fournitures médicales humanitaires destinées aux établissements de santé de la ligne de front, principalement des fournitures d’urgence de l’OMS”, a encore détaillé le dirigeant de l’agence. Depuis l’invasion russe du 24 février 2022, l’OMS a ainsi recensé 3 148 attaques contre les services de santé en Ukraine. Elles ont fait 240 morts et 1 055 blessés.

92cd6850288b5dc7.subject: Why don’t some people respond to psychedelics? 5 Questions for psychologist Rachel Ham
92cd6850288b5dc7.body:
View this post on the web at https://themicrodose.substack.com/p/why-dont-some-people-respond-to-psychedelics

For anyone who joins a clinical trial for a mental health condition, the hope is that after the trial is over, they’ll feel better. And, that their improvement will linger past the end of the research, leading to long-lasting change.
The unfortunate truth, however, is that not all treatments will be successful for everyone, nor last forever—and psychedelic-assisted therapy is no exception to that rule. Despite showing promising outcomes in clinical trials so far, some people don’t respond to psychedelic interventions.
Rachel Ham, a doctoral candidate at Monash University in Australia, has been interviewing people in a large clinical trial [ https://substack.com/redirect/5a6651b2-521e-4991-802e-c82900c8fe05?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on psilocybin and general anxiety disorder for her PhD project. She’s been learning about what the lived experience of being in a psychedelic trial is really like; she and her colleagues have been evaluating how people respond [ https://substack.com/redirect/2336f462-1ca0-4a43-89e4-787be7ddf59c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to therapeutic touch, and how they feel about having two therapists in the room [ https://substack.com/redirect/9e3d42dc-47d0-464d-b707-27932eadf3c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
In a forthcoming paper, she and her colleagues dedicated their attention to a group of low or non-responders: those who didn’t meet the threshold of a 50% reduction of their symptoms. It’s a small sample size, just seven people, but Ham thinks there’s important information to be gained from talking with them. “A motivation for us was feeling that we can learn just as much from the people who don’t have dramatic recoveries, as we can from those who do,” Ham said.
The Microdose talked to Ham about her research, and how studying limited responses can help future patients.
How do you define a psychedelic non-responder?
Psychedelic therapy has obviously shown a lot of promise, but we know that it doesn’t work for everyone. Non-response is normally defined as less than a 50% reduction in standard clinical symptom measures. We know that maybe around one-half to one-third of people meet that criteria.
For our study, we took a slightly different approach. We looked at people who did not meet that 50% symptom reduction, but we were also looking for people who had a more sustained, limited response across the whole course of their treatment.
The caveat here is when we’re dealing with real participant stories, we know that in psychedelic therapy, symptom reduction doesn’t necessarily capture everything that’s going on in this treatment. Sometimes there can be a whole host of other quality of life measures that actually improve substantially, so symptom reduction isn’t necessarily the whole picture.
And even though we often talk about “non-responders”, because this is a qualitative paper and it’s real participant stories, we’ve moved to calling them “limited responders” because it’s a little bit less pathologizing.
These limited responders go through the same therapy process as everybody else: preparation, dosing sessions, and integration. Do they just trip less? Or have less meaningful psychedelic trips? Or does their limited-response emerge later?
It’s seven participants, so we were not able to do statistical analysis, but we did look at a few acute experience measures. We looked at the challenging experiences questionnaire, the mystical experiences questionnaire, and the emotional breakthrough inventory. We compared, non-statistically, the averages between these limited responders and the broader sample. Broadly speaking, the scores are quite similar.
That’s an interesting finding out of this paper. It’s complex to make sense of, because a lot of these measures have been shown to correlate with improved therapeutic outcomes in the past. All that we can really take from that is perhaps these experiential factors don’t fully account for differences in outcomes.
Maybe there are some other pre- or post-session factors, like psychotherapeutic or relational support, that influence people meaningfully. A lot of mechanistic studies are working at a group level, so there are going to be trends. That’s very meaningful work and research. Our results caution against assuming that necessarily translates at the individual level.
How did people feel about being limited responders? Were they aware, and how did they respond?
Even within this sample, it is pretty heterogeneous. There can be quite a few different trajectories. We have three participants who show symptom scores that are increasing, which is to say that their anxiety is getting worse; we measured anxiety at three different times. And then we have four participants who actually do show reductions over time, but that did not meet the criteria for that 50% reduction.
Those are two possible trajectories of non-response. You also have another possible trajectory where someone, for example, shows a big improvement, but then has remission over time. Even within this study, we’re not necessarily capturing all of the different trajectories of limited response.
Something that we did as part of our qualitative analysis was utilize a framework that’s based around illness narratives, which explores different features of people’s storytelling in relation to their psychedelic experience and their treatment trajectory overall. A feature that we found within that was that there were some participants who tended to describe their trajectories in more sort of hopeful or future-oriented styles of narratives that kind of resembled a quest. There was something really hopeful and progress-oriented around those stories.
There were others, though, whose narratives were more marked by ambivalence and fragmentation and unresolved distress. That has been described as a chaos narrative.
These kinds of narratives might represent different stages of an ongoing therapeutic process, rather than stable endpoints.
Subscribe for more interviews and our weekly news roundup. (P.S. It’s free!)
Do you consider a limited response to be a kind of challenging psychedelic experience?
I would come back to the message that a limited response is quite heterogeneous. It’s not really a story about responders and non-responders. For a lot of people, healing is non-linear; it’s ongoing and it takes work, and that’s all deeply individual.
We did see some really challenging experiences. We had one participant that had a somatic re-experiencing of sexual assault. Another who had an emergence of a memory about childhood sexual abuse, alongside a sexuality related insight. Another witnessed violent imagery. We know that these challenging experiences have quite a lot of nuance, including what they mean in the context of psychedelic therapy and outcomes.
There’s some research by Max Wolff that looks at [ https://substack.com/redirect/dc22d758-c35d-4f95-9caa-081edee11775?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] the acceptance process during psychedelics, and how that influences outcomes. We can start to imagine some of these mechanisms might contribute to whether a challenging experience translates into benefit or or harm. Our findings raise questions around how particular forms of challenge might indicate potential vulnerability. By trying to understand these more complex trajectories, we can build models of care that are safer, more reflexive, and therefore more ethical and more effective.
Something that I think was quite interesting is that all participants felt that they had benefited from their psychedelic experiences. I don’t want to say that too flippantly, because for a lot of people, that feeling of benefit was also accompanied by quite considerable distress. You

Build an AI code review bot in 30 minutes with Vercel Eve
Listen now on YouTube [ https://substack.com/redirect/aa66ac6a-81b5-4890-bb5c-469b64072a4f?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Spotify [ https://substack.com/redirect/aa0e5a33-452b-4de9-9621-379d4a6e6e35?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] • Apple Podcasts [ https://substack.com/redirect/a007992d-9bd7-4efc-b5ae-699a02432d0e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]

WorkOS [ https://substack.com/redirect/35867ea7-450f-4b2e-82e8-280857f02e83?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]—Make your app enterprise-ready today
Claire built an AI agent that reviews pull requests, scores their risk, auto-approves the safest ones, and sends anything questionable to Slack. In this episode, she breaks down how she built the entire thing in one Codex session using Vercel Eve, and why letting AI review AI-generated code may be a lot less risky than it sounds.
Biggest takeaways:
You don’t need a human to review every AI-generated PR. That may sound reckless, but it’s increasingly looking like the smarter operating model. Intercom has already shown this can work at scale: PRs approved by its AI system move five times as fast as human-reviewed ones and have a lower revert rate. In other words, the AI-reviewed code isn’t just shipping faster—it’s less likely to need fixing after it reaches production.
The key is having a clear way to separate changes that can skip human review from ones that can’t. The risk model used here scores each PR across six dimensions: the size of the change, its blast radius, how easily it can be reversed, its data and security implications, its operational impact, and whether tests and CI have actually been completed. Anything below 24 points is classified as low risk and cleared by the agent; anything above 64 goes straight to a human for review. The exact numbers matter less than turning a vague judgment call into a repeatable system.
Vercel’s Eve may be the fastest way to deploy a serious internal AI agent across Slack and GitHub without spending weeks building infrastructure. It handles the annoying plumbing—connectors, refresh tokens, sandboxing, and routing across channels—so the actual work becomes writing instructions and skills in Markdown instead of babysitting OAuth flows.
A useful internal agent can now be built and deployed in a single Codex session, starting with a prompt that’s only a couple of sentences long. In this case, the initial ask was essentially: build a GitHub bot that waits for checks to pass; grades each PR as low, medium, or high risk; and automatically approves the low-risk ones. Everything after that was steering and refinement, not a giant up-front specification.
Browser use removes much of the configuration tax that makes agent setup feel harder than it should. Creating a Slack bot and GitHub app manually normally means clicking through endless permission screens, choosing scopes, and managing tokens. Codex handled almost all of that through the browser. The human’s job was mostly to click “save” and complete 2FA. What usually takes hours took minutes.
SOC 2 compliance and automatically approved PRs are not inherently at odds. The important part is making the process legible: the risk model needs to be reflected in the company’s code-review and security policies, every decision needs to be logged, and the resulting audit trail needs to be easy to query and defend. The security team’s role is to help design the right framework, not simply block automation because it feels unfamiliar.
The operational design matters just as much as the underlying technology. Merge Mommy doesn’t actually merge anything. Instead, it posts a gray check in GitHub as a signal, then sends a Slack message with the risk score and a note saying the PR is ready to approve and merge. That small handoff preserves human accountability for the final action while eliminating most of the cognitive work involved in reviewing a routine change.
Evals are what keep internal agents trustworthy after the novelty wears off. Intercom logs every PR review its agent produces and then has an engineer assess whether the score and recommendation were correct. That’s the same discipline strong teams already bring to customer-facing AI products. Internal agents may feel less visible, but when they touch something as important as the codebase, they need the same protection against regressions.
The surprising thing about building an Eve agent is how little “building” is actually involved. The full instructions for Merge Mommy fit on roughly a page: a few paragraphs, a handful of bullets, and a short skill file. There isn’t much framework-specific magic to learn. The core skill is simply being able to explain, clearly and precisely, what the agent should do.

She also shows how she replaced Gmail with her own Claude-powered inbox, why she believes intent engineering matters more than prompt engineering, and how non-technical people can start building useful AI workflows without writing code.

You don’t need to be technical to build a business workflow with Claude. You need to be clear about what’s broken.
